title: deportation of the Crimean Tatars
summary: The deportation of the Crimean Tatars, known as Sürgünlik, occurred from May 18 to 20, 1944, when at least 191,044 individuals were forcibly displaced by Soviet authorities under Joseph Stalin's orders. This event is a significant chapter [[coal-in-ukraine|in Ukraine]]'s history, highlighting the ethnic cleansing and cultural genocide faced by the Crimean Tatar community.

sections.heading: Historical Context
paragraphs: The [[crimean-tatars|Crimean Tatars]] governed the Crimean Khanate from 1441 until its annexation by the Russian Empire in 1783. By the 14th century, the majority of the Turkic-speaking population had adopted Islam. The Crimean Tatars frequently engaged in conflicts with Moscow, leading to waves of emigration, particularly after the Russian Empire's expansion and the [[crimean-war|Crimean War]], which saw a significant portion of the population leave for the Ottoman Empire.

sections.heading: The Deportation
paragraphs: The deportation of the Crimean Tatars was executed from May 18 to 20, 1944, under the supervision of Lavrentiy Beria and ordered by Joseph [[donetsk|Stalin]]. The NKVD utilized cattle trains to transport Crimean Tatars from [[crimea|Crimea]] to the Uzbek SSR, displacing them thousands of kilometers away. This action was framed by the Soviet government as collective punishment for alleged collaboration with Nazi Germany during World War II, despite evidence showing that many Crimean Tatars fought for the Soviet Red Army.

sections.heading: Consequences of the Deportation
paragraphs: By the end of the deportation, no Crimean Tatars remained in Crimea, resulting in the abandonment of 80,000 houses and 360,000 acres of land. Approximately 8,000 Crimean Tatars died during the deportation, with many more succumbing to the harsh conditions of exile. Following the deportation, the Soviet government initiated a campaign to erase [[crimean-tatar|Crimean Tatar]] culture and presence.

sections.heading: Post-War Developments
paragraphs: In 1956, [[nikita-khrushchev|Nikita Khrushchev]] criticized Stalin's policies but did not allow the Crimean Tatars to return to their homeland. It was not until the late 1980s, during the perestroika era, that 260,000 Crimean Tatars returned to Crimea after 45 years of exile. On November 14, 1989, the Supreme Council of [[soviet-union|the Soviet Union]] officially recognized the deportations as a crime.

sections.heading: Recognition and Legacy
paragraphs: By 2004, Crimean Tatars constituted 12% of Crimea's population, although they received no assistance or compensation from the Soviet government for their losses. The deportation and subsequent assimilation efforts are pivotal events in Crimean Tatar history. Between 2015 and 2025, several countries, including [[ukraine|Ukraine]], formally recognized the deportation as genocide.
